raw_comment:
I notice that there seems to be a clear negative trend in the ages of world leaders, over the past 70 years. In 1950, the average age of world leaders seemed to be around 62, whereas in 2020, it seems to have dropped to around 52.  The spread in ages of world leaders does not seem to have changed though, as the spread appears to be around 20 years above and below the average across all years. Another thing I noticed is that Republican U.S. presidents appear to generally be older than Democrat U.S. presidents, as most of the republican presidents are above the trend line and most democrat presidents are below the trend line in age. 
I wonder why Republican presidents tend to be older than Democrat presidents, and I also wonder if there are distinct differences in ages based on parties for other countries. I wonder what may explain these differences in age based on party affiliation, and if age could somehow be correlated to presidential election winners based on party. I also wonder if the trend line is statistically significant in the model.
This impacts my community and me as it shows that in general, world leaders have been younger and younger over the years, as this could perhaps impact who a candidate may relate to most. 
“Changes in Average Ages of World Leaders Over Time”

I notice that the trend for the ages of world leaders is decreasing. This surprised me because the 2024 election has created a common opinion that the two candidates are too old. Whether or not that is true, it is interesting to see that that has, in fact, happened before, and even to a further extent with Churchill being 80 when elected. This trend directly impacts the world, as the age of leaders changes a nation's stability and power.

- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the ages of US Presidents follow a similar trend as the ages of the leaders of foreign nations. Overall, the average age of  presidents and prime ministers has decreased from the 1950 to 2020. Additionally, almost every single Democratic president is younger than the average trend, while almost every Republican president has been older than the average trend.   
What do you wonder?
I wonder if the trend line will begin to rise again after eight years of having a president over the age of 70, especially if Biden, a 78 year-old,  is elected. Will the trend continue to rise after the election of 2024? 
What impact does this have on you and your community?
Even though the trendline has decreased, the average age of a president is still much above the median age of the United States population - 37.9 years. People of older generations have much different values than those of younger ones. Hence, most presidents are not in touch with the issues that are most pressing to my generation and personal community.

raw_comment:
1.  I noticed that Churchill is the oldest president on the 
       graph, while Kennedy is the youngest.  The range of 
       president and prime minister ages is about 33 years.  A 
       general observation can be made that most democratic 
       presidents were younger in age while in office compared 
       to Republican presidents.  The overall trend line shows 
       that as years pass by the age of presidents is decreasing.  
       This trend does not necessarily represent the current 
       happenings in more recent years.
2. I wonder why the graph is comparing U.S presidents to 
       other nations.  By comparing ages of multiple nations, 
       does it relate to the views and effectiveness of leadership 
       by these elected officials? Does the age of a president or 
       prime minister represent the views of the nation they 
       govern? 
3.    Different aged elected officials share different views.  
       Younger presidents will appeal and relate more closely to 
       younger citizens.  Older presidents will appeal more to 
       older citizens.  As political views and techniques change 
       over time, candidates regardless of age need to relate to 
       all citizens for everyone's best interest.  However, 
       different aged presidents face different challenges during 
       election and once elected. 
4.  What does Age represent? Do older and younger elected 
      officials face the same challenges

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |
raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  "Our Leaders Are the Grandparents of Nations" by Frank of Milford, Delaware, “Presidents: Old and Experienced, or Young and Innovative?“ by Sam of Academy of Saint Elizabeth, "Are the Older Bolder, or Will They Smolder?" by Bella of USA, "Age Is Just a Number, But Does It Influence the President?" by Sophie of Andover, Massachusetts, and “Are US Presidents Too Old?” by Morgan of Tulsa, Oklahoma.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow afternoon Thursday, Oct. 29 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or
a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs). 

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized:
By topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex),
By graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and
By Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who thinks age is only one factor that determines who could be a great leader,  and Greg Yarnall of Morristown, New Jersey, who has definitely aged more than 7 months since March...

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |
raw_comment:
I noticed that Churchill was the oldest in office, while Kennedy was the youngest in office. If Biden were to be elected, he would be the oldest president entering office. I also notice that the majority of democratic presidents fall under the trend line (Truman doesn't), while republican presidents either cross or are past the trend line. Based on the gray arrows, it also seems like the youngest leader of a democratic nation is well below the age of forty, and the oldest leader of a democratic nation well over the age of eighty. 
I wonder why the average age has a downward trend, as shown by the trend line. I wonder how age relates - if at all - to the way that democratic leaders govern their nation. I also wonder whether age affects the nation's views of the president/PM, and if it plays in a role in voting. I wonder how this graph would compare if leaders of non-democratic nations were included. Since elected democrats tend to be younger than elected republicans, I wonder why that is. Is it because conservative and liberal ideals appeal differently between generations? 
This impacts my community because if age correlates to the decisions that leaders make in office, then if affects us, the population that they're governing. Younger candidates will appeal more to younger generations such as Gen Z and millennials and be lost in touch in with older generations such as Gen X and boomers. 
Headline: Is Age Just a Number? The Downward Trend of Age for Democratic Nation Leaders.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |
raw_comment:
Sorry...We looked at this with a Canadian perspective.

What do you notice?
All ages on this graph are over 40.
It shows all Presidents from 1950 to 2020, including Presidential candidates.
Only Trump and Biden have a circle at the end.
There is only one presidential candidate.
The average age of leaders (the trend) is going down with the exception of American leaders.
Blue represents the Democratic party.
Red represents the Republican party. 

What do you wonder?
Why weren't more heads of state included from other countries?  
Why are more Democrats younger than Republicans?

Suggested Headline:
World Leaders: Are newer generations picking younger leaders?

Other:
The data displayed does not match the title, making the information in this graph biased. There are only 3 heads of state from England, and one from Canada. Therefore is not an appropriate comparable when there are 14 American points of data.

Sorry.

- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**

- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)

| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |
raw_comment:
Democratic Leaders: The club of the young(er)?

The ages of presidents and prime ministers has slowly decreased since 1950, with obvious outliers. I wonder why most of the leaders are older than 40? I wonder if age requirments for each nation changes the age of the leaders? I wonder why the graph only shows the ages of democratic nations. Does it have anything to do with the length of term served as leader of nation? I wonder why most of the blue arrows are below the line,  while red arrows are above. The graph shows us the age of our prime ministers and presidents of our respective countries. The decrease in the ages of leaders could show that age is becoming less of a factor when regarding if one is capable of being a leader. It could also means that the younger leaders can connect with the youth easier, though the two current presidential candidates are older than 70.

raw_comment:
We are a class of 7th and 8th graders. 
We noticed:
 - A lot of old men
 - Some arrows are longer than others - they seem to match the length of time in office. 
 - There are red (US Republicans), gray (other countries), and blue (U.S. Democrats) arrows.  
 - The trend is between 60-70 years old.  
 - JFK was the youngest. 
 - Biden would be the oldest on the graph if elected. 
 - The average age decreases as time goes by, with the exception of Trump (and possibly Biden)
 - Most of the arrows below the trend line are blue, and most of the arrows above the line are red. 

We wonder:
 - when there will be a female president.
 - why more people over 50 get elected.
 - who the unlabeled arrows represent, and how many countries are represented
 
The impact this has on us and our community is that the President has a lot of influence -  If just old people are president, then new perspectives are never brought to the table and we just keep repeating the same old thing. An older candidate might not be able to connect and empathize with younger people.

Some headlines:
 - The Old and the Older: How the American Presidents' Ages Compare to Other Countries' Leaders
 - Old is the New Young; America Wake Up!
 - Presidency is Reaching a New Age

|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice that many of the US's republican presidents are over the age of sixty, while many of the US's democratic presidents are younger than the age of sixty. I also notice that a large amount of  government leaders from other nations' ages have gone down over time from 1950-2020.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why there is a trend of old republicans being president and young democrats being the president. I wonder why that is? Why isn't it the other way around? I also wonder why the rest of the world is getting younger leaders through the years? 

Title for the graph?

Old Republican Leaders, Young Democratic Leaders, International Leaders are Getting Younger.

raw_comment:
By examining this graph, I notice that the past and present presidents of the United States varied in ages from about to 50-80 years old. In examining the trends, the United States Presidents seem to not really follow any trend. I also think it is interesting that most prime ministers are all above the age of 65 besides the Canada Prime Minister. I wonder why it is so common for older men and women to want to run for office. Is it because candidates assume the most votes will go to the older candidate because they appear to be wiser? It appears nowadays that most young candidates in the US usually never get far when running for president. There might be a correlation between the stereotypical idea of a president being older which causes citizens to feel uneasy with a younger president. 
This impacts my community because as the millennials and generation z begin to get older, it appears we agree more with younger, more progressive candidates. If most head of governments appear to be older, our voices and opinions might not be heard. Because these generations grew up in times of social media and these modern times, our views on a lot of issues differ greatly than the older generations. 
Headline: "As Millennials and Generation Z Age, Will We See Younger Candidates"

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

The Presidential election is in six days.  There are so many graphs of polls and the positions of the candidates and their supporters.  Rather than a graph on these aspects of the election, here is a graph about the ages of O.E.C.D. (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) world leaders since 1950.  What is the trend of the ages of world leaders when they are in office?  And, how do the ages of our candidates compare to the  ages of recent world leaders?  

Here are a couple words you may want to check for your understanding and use in your response:  gerontocracy, ageism, Baby Boomers, and presidential vs. parliamentary systems.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Finally, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the graph. 

By Friday, we’ll reveal the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  Reply even after you have read the Reveal.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |
raw_comment:
I notice that Republican Presidents tended to be older than Democrat Presidents. The three oldest US presidents, as of right now, are all Republican. 

I wonder how age affects the Presidents or a leader of a countries ability to govern? Is it a good thing because they are older and have more experience? Or is it a bad thing because sometimes older politicians can be out of touch with issues affecting the youth.

This impacts me because we are a week away from one of the biggest and most heated United States presidential elections. Both candidates, Biden and Trump, are in their 70's. Their ages are considered old compared to other presidents in US history. As a young person, I hope they will listen to issues Gen-Z is facing and not ignore young people. Especially the issue of the American Education System.

Presidents: old and experienced, or young and innovative?

## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
Most Republican Presidents are above or on the trendline age. The oldest Republican Presidents were Reagan and Trump, with Bush being slightly older. The Democratic Party has their Presidents being under the trendline age with the only outliers above the trend being Truman or possibly Biden and Kennedy being the youngest outlier. The Democratic Party shows the trend of their Presidents becoming younger with time, while Republicans remain 55 years old or older. 

What do you wonder?
Does the Democratic Party want to represent the younger generations more by picking younger candidates (excluding Biden). 
 
What impact does this have on you and your community?
A divide between the younger generations and older generations will continue unless representation of both age groups occurs. Younger political members, like AOC, are generally hated amongst the older population from seeming like they know nothing, while the younger people love to see someone they could possibly connect to. Older political leaders appreciation is then flipped, with the older population loving a leader near their age and the younger people believing the leader is "delusional". This just creates a divide and continues to stir arguments between people because of the drastic age demographic representation. 

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
"Does Age Really Matter?"

- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**

- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**

- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**

- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |
